title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 27
paragraphs: So they spoke, and the Athenians replied: “Though we know this gathering was assembled for battle with the barbarian and not for speeches, yet since the Tegean has set us the task of speaking of things both old and new — the deeds of merit achieved by each of our two nations through all time — we must point out to you from what source it is that we, who have always been brave men, have the chief place as a heritage rather than the Arcadians. First, as to the sons of Heracles — whose leader they claim to have killed at the Isthmus — in earlier times, when they were being driven away by all the Greeks to whom they had fled to escape slavery under the Myceneans, we alone received them, and joining with them we subdued the insolence of Eurystheus, defeating in battle those who then dwelt in the Peloponnese. Again, when the Argives who marched with Polyneikes against Thebes had been killed and lay unburied, we declare that we marched an army against the Cadmeians and recovered the dead bodies, burying them in our own land at Eleusis. We have another glorious deed performed against the Amazons who once invaded Attica from the river Thermodon. And in the toils of Troy we were inferior to none. But it is no use making mention of these things — for though we were brave men then, we might by now have become worthless; or though we were worthless then, we might be better now. Let what concerns ancient deeds suffice. But even if we had displayed no other deed (though many glorious ones there are, no fewer than any other Greek people's), by reason of the deed accomplished at Marathon alone we are worthy to have this privilege, and others besides — for we alone of all the Greeks fought in single combat with the Persian, and having undertaken so great a task, we overcame and defeated forty-six nations. Are we not worthy, then, to hold this post on that deed alone? However, since at such a time as this it is not fitting to contend for a post, we are ready to follow what you say, Lacedaemonians, as to where you think it most suitable for us to stand and against whom; for wherever we are posted, we shall try to be brave men. Prescribe to us, then, and we shall obey.” Thus they answered; and the whole body of Lacedaemonians shouted aloud that the Athenians were more worthy to hold the wing than the Arcadians. So the Athenians got the wing and overcame the Tegeans.
